title: What burpsy does not do
summary: Every row is a decision, not a defect — and each one is a way a result can be narrower than it looks. Read this before reading a quiet scan as an absent vulnerability.
source: ROADMAP.md § Deliberately out of scope; burpsy-go/ui-gaps.md; each row re-checked against the code

rows.detail: BCheck's interactions operator has no interaction server behind it. The 26 corpus checks that use it are counted into a Collaborator bucket when the corpus loads and are never dispatched.
rows.note: generate_collaborator_address() is deliberately not stubbed: an address nothing polls would convert all 26 into silent false negatives. The catalog's own OOB rows — SSRF, blind SQLi, XXE, the three external-service-interaction issues — do run, but only when the interactsh-client binary is on PATH; without it they decline with a reason instead of reporting clean.

rows.detail: The proxy blind-tunnels CONNECT and records one message-less row with tls: true. The requests inside that tunnel are never in HTTP history, and nothing scans them.
rows.note: The same is true per host for anything matched by TLS passthrough. /ca.crt answers 404 and the status bar reads "no CA" when interception is off, so the console never offers a certificate it cannot hand out.

rows.term: Parse rate is not run rate
rows.detail: All 264 published BCheck files parse. That number says nothing about how many reached a verdict against your traffic.
rows.note: GET /api/scanner/coverage reports every loaded check as never dispatched, ran clean, ran and found, or errored, with a reason for each skip. With nothing loaded it says so rather than implying a clean scan.

rows.detail: Impossible: no JVM, and no binary or source compatibility with MontoyaApi. There is no plugin surface of any kind — the extension phase was never shipped.
rows.note: Of userInterface()'s registration points, the ten Swing ones are out of scope for lack of an honest web analogue. The three declarative ones — context-menu items, message-editor tabs, menu actions — are in scope.

rows.detail: The capture store is append-only. It has put, add and annotate, and no delete of any kind; History's filters hide rows and remove nothing.
Same store, same property: the site map adds and never removes. A host on the map was observed at some point — that is not evidence it is reachable now.
Six of Burp's 29 shipped configurations set a key this engine implements, and there are no custom-config knobs, so there is no configuration wizard — it would offer controls that do nothing.
rows.note: The working path is the row context menu's "Audit exchange", or Target → Issues → targeted audit with the config selector.

rows.detail: importBambda takes Java source. The filter substrate here is the closed typed grammar above, deliberately not a scripting engine.
rows.note: The route answers 400 with a grammar reference — never {"imported": true} for something that was never executed.

rows.detail: Burp's exportProjectFileAndExit, loadProjectFile and restart all presuppose a project file. Durable state here is a capture directory plus a SQLite mirror, which is a different object.
rows.note: project().name() returns null on purpose. A name derived from the -db filename would land in report headers as if an operator had chosen it.

rows.detail: The exchange record carries no IP field, so History cannot show one. A column filled from a fresh lookup would report where the host resolves now, not where the request went.
Absent. Burp loops the response back through its own listener and burpsy has no loopback surface, so the menu item does not exist rather than existing and failing.
Not shipped, in this port or in the Rust reference. The JSON API is what drives burpsy today; docs/MCP.md records the plan as a plan.

A native window ships: cmd/desktop is a Wails v2 shell with a native File/View/Tools/Help menu bar, native dialogs and the same console UI served over a reverse proxy. There is no system tray, and the browser page on the -web address remains the headless path — burpsy stays usable over SSH without the shell.

Out of scope as derivative work. Checks are implemented from the published specs and the public BCheck and Montoya contracts instead — which is also why the corpus is loaded at runtime rather than vendored.
Out of scope. Several are Enterprise-only in Burp itself and have no desktop-product behaviour to match.

title: Query language
summary: The filter grammar over captured traffic. One small closed typed language, shared by the History filter box and the CLI's history --query.
source: internal/query — grammar and rationale in query.go's package doc

blocks.label: Grammar
blocks.body:
query      := or-expr
or-expr    := and-expr ( "or" and-expr )*
and-expr   := unary-expr ( "and" unary-expr )*
unary-expr := "not" unary-expr | primary
primary    := "(" or-expr ")" | comparison
comparison := field op value
field      := "host" | "status" | "method" | "path" | "mime" | "body"
            | "length" | "duration" | "extension" | "params"
            | "highlight" | "comment" | "task" | "header" "[" string "]"

blocks.label: Examples
blocks.body:
host = api.example.com
host ~ example
status = 500
status != 304
status >= 400
status in 500..599
method = POST
path ~ /admin
task = 3
task != 0
mime ~ json
length > 1mb
length in 1kb..1mb
length = 0
duration > 500ms
duration in 100ms..2s
header["server"] ~ "nginx"
header["set-cookie"] ~ "HttpOnly"
not header["strict-transport-security"] ~ "max-age"
extension = "js"
params > 3
highlight = "red"
highlight = ""
comment ~ "injectable"
body ~ password
host = api.example.com and status >= 400
method = POST or method = PUT
not path ~ /static and status = 200
(host ~ api or host ~ auth) and status >= 500
host = "8080"

rows.detail: = (or ==), != and ~ (contains), each against a string value.
rows.note: host and mime fold case — DNS names and MIME types both are case-insensitive. method and path do not, because the method token is case-sensitive per RFC 7230 and the path per RFC 3986; folding either would accept a query describing a different wire request than the one sent.

rows.detail: = (or ==), !=, <, <=, >, >= with an integer, or in low..high for a range inclusive of both ends.
rows.note: A literal outside 0-65535 is refused at parse time. An inverted range (status in 299..200) parses and matches nothing — the bounds are compared, not reordered.

rows.detail: ~ only, matched case-sensitively against the raw response bytes.
Response size in bytes: = (or ==), !=, <, <=, >, >= and in low..high. Accepts b, kb, mb and gb; a bare number means bytes.
rows.note: length = 0 is a real answer — a 204 is zero-length — so it does not match a request still waiting, which has no length at all. An inverted range (length in 1mb..1kb) is refused at parse time rather than matching nothing.

rows.detail: Your own annotations on a row: =, != and ~ (contains), all case-insensitive.
rows.note: The only fields here describing burpsy's state rather than the target's, and the only ones where "" is a real answer — highlight = "" asks for rows you have not triaged. Everywhere else an empty value means the target gave us nothing and fails every comparison. A consumer that cannot answer at all (the crawler's frontier gate, a match/replace candidate) still fails every comparison including the empty one, so a queued URL is never reported as an untriaged exchange.

rows.detail: Derived from the path: extension takes =, != and ~ case-insensitively; params is a count and takes the numeric operators.
rows.note: Both are computed from the path rather than sent, so they cannot disagree between rows — and they use the same rules as the History table's Extension and Query columns (pathParts), so the filter and the column beside it always agree. params counts QUERY parameters only; Burp's Params column also counts body parameters, which are not on an index row. A path with no extension matches NO extension comparison, negations included.

rows.detail: A response header: = (or ==), != and ~ (contains). The name is quoted and matched case-insensitively; so is the value.
rows.note: Indexed rather than a flat text match over the whole head, which would let a match straddle a header boundary. Any-of over repeated values, because Set-Cookie repeats and "does any cookie contain HttpOnly" is the question. An absent header fails EVERY comparison including !=, so ask for absence with not header["x"] ~ "y". A header present with an empty value is not absent.

rows.detail: How long the exchange took: the same operators as length. Accepts us, ms and s; a bare number means milliseconds, matching the History column.
rows.note: An exchange nobody timed matches NO duration comparison, negations included. burpsy records whether a duration was measured rather than defaulting to zero, so an untimed exchange is never reported as instantaneous.

rows.term: Absent fields are absent, not zero
rows.detail: A request with no response yet has status 0, mime "", no length and no duration, and every comparison on an absent field is false — never true, never an error.
rows.note: This is why status != 304 does not include pending rows: they have no status to differ from. Before it was explicit, status < 400 matched every request still waiting, because 0 < 400. length and duration carry the same rule through an explicit presence flag rather than a sentinel value, because 0 bytes and 0 microseconds are both real answers.

rows.detail: not binds tightest, then and, then or — so a or b and c parses as a or (b and c). Parentheses override both.
Quoted values support exactly five escapes: \", \\, \n, \t and \r. An unrecognised escape is a parse error rather than a silently dropped backslash.
rows.note: An unquoted bare word is accepted as a string (host = example.com). The Rust reference requires quotes; this is a named divergence, not an accident.

rows.detail: The History filter box sends the expression to the server; the CLI takes the same text as history --query. The crawler frontier gate refuses a query naming a field it cannot honestly evaluate before a response exists.

title: BCheck syntax
summary: PortSwigger's check DSL, parsed and evaluated in full. Burp's scan checks are largely data rather than code, so one interpreter inherits the published corpus instead of porting hundreds of Java checks.

blocks.label: A complete check
blocks.body:
metadata:
    language: v2-beta
    name: "Readable .git directory"
    description: "Requests .git/HEAD and reports a readable Git repository"
    author: "burpsy"
    tags: "exposure", "misconfiguration"

define:
    probe = "/.git/HEAD"

given host then
    send request called head:
        method: "GET"
        replacing path: {probe}
        appending headers:
            "Accept": "*/*"

    if {head.response.status_code} is "200"
       and {head.response.body} contains "ref:" then
        report issue:
            severity: medium
            confidence: firm
            detail: "The Git repository is served at {probe}."
            remediation: "Deny requests for /.git from the web root."
    end if

rows.detail: Start burpsy with -bchecks DIR. The corpus is deliberately not vendored into this repository — you supply the directory, and the loader reports what it read.
language, name, description, author, severity, confidence, and tags / reference (comma-separated). Unknown keys are tolerated as v2-beta extensions rather than refused.
name = value pairs, comma-separated. Referenced elsewhere as {name}. define: and run for each: may appear in either order.
name = v1, v2, … — the check body runs once per combination.
rows.note: Bounded at 10,000 entries per list and 100,000 across the cartesian product, so a hostile check cannot turn the evaluator into a denial of service.

rows.detail: One of: response, host, request, path, or insertion point. An insertion-point check may name the kinds it wants — any, query, header, body or cookie, joined by or — as in given query or header insertion point then.
rows.note: given response with no send and no run tool is what makes a check passive; everything else is active. The published corpus splits 104 response, 98 host, 40 request, 11 path.

rows.detail: Either a raw literal or template string, or clauses of replacing / appending plus a target — method, path, query_string, queries, headers or body. send request called NAME: binds the result as {NAME.response…}.
rows.note: Replacing path leaves the query string intact, because the grammar exposes path and query_string as separate targets. That is an inference from the grammar, not an observation of Burp's runtime, and it is marked as such in the code.

rows.term: if … then / else if / else / end if
rows.detail: end if is the only block terminator. Whitespace and newlines are insignificant, and # starts a comment to end of line.
is, matches (RE2), contains, in, differs from, eq, ne — combined with and, or, not and parentheses. <any|dns|http|smtp> interactions polls a Collaborator.
rows.note: An absent operand makes a comparison false, never true. Coercing an unresolvable path to the empty string once made {missing} in {latest.response} report on every response, because contains("") is true.

rows.detail: severity (high, medium, low, info) and confidence (certain, firm, tentative) are required; name, detail and remediation are optional.
Two different messages once anything has been sent. Every send updates latest; before the first send they are the same exchange.
rows.note: Every send is built from base.request, never from the previous send — a second send payload is base plus payload, not payload plus payload. Modifiers accumulate within one send request; sends do not accumulate.

rows.term: A failed send abandons the check
rows.detail: Continuing would leave {check.response} absent and invite exactly the false positive the absence rules prevent. The failure is counted, not swallowed.

A given insertion point check runs once per point and mutates exactly one, so a finding is attributable to a single parameter. Outside such a check the finding's Parameter column is empty on purpose — a per-host finding is about a resource, not a parameter.
rows.note: Nested insertion points are deliberately not enumerated: a miss, never a false positive. any includes headers, which the JWT checks depend on.

rows.detail: Shells out to an external binary, so it is never passive. Not dispatched unless burpsy was started with -tools name=/abs/path; without a runner it is counted at load and refused.

title: Tables
summary: What every table in the console does, whichever tool it belongs to.

rows.detail: Select one row, toggle one, or select the range from the last plain click. Ranges follow the rows as displayed — sorted and filtered.
rows.note: Opt-in per table: History, Logger and the site map's request table have it.

rows.detail: Extend the selection from the keyboard; select every displayed row (with the table focused).
Keeps the selection and offers the N-row menu: Send to Comparer (A and B), Copy URLs, Add to Organizer, Add hosts to scope, and the table's own bulk actions.
Copy <column> column (every loaded row's value), Hide <column> column, Restore default table layout.
Show or hide columns; the choice is remembered per table.
Reorder columns; the order is remembered per table.
History, Logger and Organizer: restore defaults, save the filter as a named preset or to a file, and load either back.
History: jump to a row by its # number; says when the row is filtered out, older than the loaded rows, or gone.

title: Proxy history
summary: The HTTP history row menu (and the same menu on the site map's request table).

rows.term: Send to Repeater / Intruder / Sequencer / Decoder
rows.detail: Hand the exchange's request to that tool. Repeater opens a new tab; the others seed their input.
Load the request into one side of Comparer.
Change request method, change body encoding, toggle chunked framing — each on a copy in a new Repeater tab; the history row never changes.

rows.term: Copy URL / Copy as curl / Copy as sqlmap command / Copy links
rows.detail: The URL; a curl or sqlmap command with the request's headers and body; every link the response carries.

rows.term: Copy request to file / Save request and response
rows.detail: Download the request alone, or both halves in one labelled file.
Annotate the row; both are filterable (highlight and comment are query fields).

rows.term: Add to Organizer / Add to site map
rows.detail: Keep the exchange in Organizer; record its URL on the site map without sending anything.
The request and response in a separate window (also: double-click a row).
Replace the query with host = <host>.

rows.term: Open URL in browser / Show response in browser
rows.detail: Fetch the URL through burpsy's browser, or serve this exchange's stored response as-is.
An include rule for the host. The status bar's rule count updates.

rows.term: Audit exchange / Actively scan this branch or host (crawl)
rows.detail: Queue an active audit of this exchange, or crawl from it.

rows.term: Record an issue / Generate CSRF PoC
rows.detail: Record a finding against this exchange; open an auto-submitting PoC page for it.
Multi-row menu: remove the rows from the history view, after a confirmation.
rows.note: Burp's Delete item; the underlying capture is not renumbered.

summary: The frame and connection menus on Proxy › WebSockets history.

rows.detail: Open the connection in a Repeater WebSocket tab.
Hand one frame's payload to that tool.

rows.term: Copy frame summary / frame id / exchange id
rows.detail: Identifiers and a one-line description for notes and tickets.
The frame's payload bytes, as a download.

rows.term: Show this exchange in HTTP history
rows.detail: Jump to the upgrade request that opened the connection.

title: Site map
summary: The site map tree's node menu; its request table uses the Proxy history menu.

rows.detail: Open or close every folder under the node. Expanding stops at 5,000 folders and says how many stayed closed.
An include rule for the node's host.
Re-read the stored traffic under the node through the passive checks; nothing is sent.
Crawl from the node, retained to its host or branch.

rows.term: Copy URLs in this host / branch
rows.detail: Every URL under the node, one per line.
The issues found under the node.
Hide the node from the map, after a confirmation.
rows.note: Suppression, not deletion: the captured bytes stay in the store.

rows.detail: A URL is in scope when an enabled include rule matches it and no enabled exclude rule does.
Proxy history, the site map and Logger rows all offer Add <host> to scope.

title: Message editor
summary: The request/response editor's menu, in every tool that shows a message.

rows.detail: URL, HTML and Base64 encode or decode the selected text (Ctrl+U/H/B, Shift to decode). A read-only message shows the result in a dialog.
Mint a payload and insert it at the cursor (editable messages).
Intruder's base request: mark the selection as a payload position.
Raw view: audit only the selected bytes as the insertion point.
Open the editor's search panel (Ctrl+S).

rows.detail: Pretty reformats only the display; the bytes sent are Raw's.
Ctrl+S search, Ctrl+, / Ctrl+. previous/next match, Ctrl+D delete line, Ctrl+Up/Down paragraph, Ctrl+Alt+C copy prettified.
